posts.title: Happy Tenth Anniversary, Spoonie Authors Network!
posts.description: Photo by Cup of Couple on Pexels.com Cait Gordon here, also known as “your humble SpAN Editor” and Spoonie Author Network founder! Mid-November reminds me that yet another year has passed for the Spoonie Authors Network. And this year marks a decade since I founded this community initiative. Why did I do it in the first place? I was a newly published author who was disabled, and after I attended my first writers’ conference, I felt inspired to connect with other creatives who managed spoons. I created this website and hoped if I built it, they would come. And the contributing authors came! They gave their time and offered their words through articles and interviews, understanding this was a community of volunteers who felt inspired to share their realities as Spoonies. I will be forever grateful for them. Some of our authors included Dr. Derek Newman-Stille, ’Nathan Burgoine, Stephen Graham King, Christina Robins (C.L. posts.title: Featured Author: Cait Gordon
posts.description: Cait Gordon Cait Gordon is an award-winning speculative fiction author and anthologist. She founded The Spoonie Authors Network in 2016, a community initiative of volunteers who give of their time to share their experiences as disabled creatives. She’s advocated for disabled voices in literary spaces for over ten years. Cait wrote the 2023 Indie Ink Award–winning, disability-hopepunk adventure, Season One: Iris and the Crew Tear Through Space! Her short stories featuring disabled and/or queer heroes appear in the multiple-nominated collection, Speculative Shorts: Stories that fell out of my brain . Hot Wings and Sauciness , starring an autistic, disabled, and sweary female lead, is her latest novel. Cait twice joined Talia C. Johnson to co-edit the multi-genre, disability fiction anthologies: Nothing Without Us (a Prix Aurora Award finalist) and Nothing Without Us Too (a Prix Aurora Award winner). She is also the host of The Disabled Crone podcast.

posts.title: It’s Invisible Disabilities Week and yes, you do matter!
posts.description: Photo by Farman Kareem on Pexels.com (I chose this image because sunflowers are often the symbol of invisible or hidden disabilities.) I’ve been reminded on the socials that it’s Invisible Disabilities Week. And this is something that’s very personal to me. While these days you will most likely see me with Noola, my trusty rollator, before my disability became easily perceived, it was “invisible” for years. And it was not alone. Invisible disability is a term for disabilities that aren’t always noticeable or obvious. They are often accompanied by reactions like, “Are you sure you’re sick?” or “But you look so healthy!” or “Well, you’re not like my friend in a wheelchair who is really disabled!” (Yeah, it’s always super fun being on the receiving end of those types of questions or remarks.)
